name: Diseases Caused by Gram-Negative Enteric Bacilli

clinicalPearls: The enteric gram-negative bacilli (GNB) that most often cause extraintestinal infection belong to the order Enterobacterales and include Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterobacter, Serratia, Citrobacter, Morganella, Providencia, Cronobacter, and Edwardsiella; Salmonella, Shigella, and Yersinia are covered separately as mainly enteric pathogens.

Isolation of a GNB from a normally sterile site almost always signifies true infection, whereas recovery from nonsterile sites (open wounds, respiratory tract, catheterized urine) needs clinical correlation because it may represent only colonization.

E. coli and, to a lesser extent, Klebsiella are the most virulent of this group and can cause severe disease even in previously healthy ambulatory people; the other genera behave mainly as opportunists in long-term-care and hospitalized patients.

The urinary tract is the single most common extraintestinal site infected by extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli (ExPEC), and E. coli is the leading uropathogen across essentially all UTI syndromes and host groups.

The urinary tract is also the most common source of E. coli bacteremia (roughly one-half to two-thirds of episodes); the abdomen is the second most common source (about one-quarter), and some abdominal sources such as abscesses can be clinically silent and require imaging.
E. coli and group B Streptococcus are leading causes of neonatal meningitis; most neonatal E. coli meningitis strains carry the K1 capsular antigen, and ventriculomegaly is a common complication.

Hypervirulent K. pneumoniae (hvKp), first recognized in Taiwan in 1986, classically presents as community-acquired monomicrobial pyogenic liver abscess in patients without prior hepatobiliary disease, often diabetic, with a striking tendency to spread metastatically (e.g., endophthalmitis, brain/splenic/prostatic abscess, meningitis, necrotizing fasciitis).

Proteus produces urease, which hydrolyzes urea to ammonia and alkalinizes the urine; this promotes struvite and carbonate-apatite crystals, catheter biofilms, and staghorn calculi, and the organism typically cannot be cleared without removing the stone or catheter.

Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) are classified by CDC and WHO as an urgent, critical-priority threat and were estimated to cause more than 100,000 deaths globally in 2019, with the heaviest burden in low- and middle-income regions such as the Indian subcontinent.
Pneumonia, sepsis, and septic shock arising from any GNB focus are especially dangerous, carrying reported mortality rates of about 20 to 60 percent.

Serratia marcescens is notable for environmental and outbreak associations (contaminated infusates, prefilled syringes, soaps, even chlorhexidine); some strains produce red pigment that can cause distinctive findings such as pink breast milk, pink hypopyon, or pseudohemoptysis.

In children with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC/EHEC) infection, antibiotics should be avoided because they may increase the risk of hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS), and adequate volume expansion may help protect the kidneys.
harrison.pathophysiology: Enteric GNB are predominantly extracellular pathogens that normally reside in the colonic microbiota and environmental niches. Their outer membrane (lipopolysaccharide and capsule) is central both to virulence and to antimicrobial resistance via permeability barriers and efflux pumps. Disease requires accessory virulence genes: multiple adhesins (e.g., type 1, S, and F1C fimbriae and P pili in E. coli) for attachment; iron-acquisition systems (siderophores) and other nutrient-scavenging tools; capsule and O-antigen to resist complement and phagocytosis in the absence of antibody; and toxins (e.g., E. coli hemolysin) that cause tissue damage facilitating spread. The lipid A moiety of lipopolysaccharide acts as a PAMP that, through pattern-recognition receptors, can trigger an exuberant proinflammatory cascade leading to septic shock, with DAMPs such as HMGB1 propagating injury. Extensive antigenic variation (E. coli alone has more than 150 O, ~80 K, and ~53 H antigens) permits immune evasion and repeated infection and has hampered vaccine development. Host defenses are innate (intact skin/mucosa, complement, antimicrobial peptides, phagocytes, nutrient withholding) and humoral; impairment of these increases both susceptibility and severity. Intestinal pathogenic E. coli use distinct, pathotype-specific mechanisms (Shiga toxin, heat-stable/labile enterotoxins, attaching-and-effacing lesions, epithelial invasion, aggregative adherence).

infectionMimics: Colonization without infection (positive sputum culture without pneumonia, or bacteriuria without UTI), which can be mistaken for active infection particularly in elderly or functionally compromised patients
Other urea-splitting uropathogens producing alkaline urine and struvite stones
Polymicrobial intraabdominal and soft-tissue infections in which the pathogenic role of any single GNB is uncertain
nonInfectiousMimics: Scombroid (fish) poisoning, in which Proteus-mediated histamine generation in spoiled fish produces a histamine-toxicity syndrome rather than infection

additionalInvestigations: Culture of the primary site of infection before starting antimicrobials, plus blood cultures in systemically ill patients
MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, nucleic acid amplification tests, sequencing, and immunoassays for rapid organism identification and detection of resistance genes
Genotypic and phenotypic carbapenemase detection to guide infection control and therapy
Cross-sectional imaging (e.g., CT) to find occult abdominal sources such as abscesses underlying bacteremia

For suspected STEC/EHEC: CDC recommends evaluating all community-acquired diarrhea by simultaneous stool culture plus detection of Shiga toxin or its genes, since bloody stool and fecal leukocytes are not reliably present

Identification of the five biomarkers iucA, iroB, peg-344, rmpA, and rmpA2 is currently the most accurate way to identify hypervirulent K. pneumoniae; the string/hypermucoviscosity test is suboptimally sensitive and specific
Sorbitol-nonfermentation screening with serotyping and Shiga toxin testing to identify O157 STEC
redFlags: Fever and/or back/flank pain in a patient with cystitis, suggesting progression to pyelonephritis
Persistently rising fever, flank pain, and neutrophilia during treated pyelonephritis, prompting evaluation for intrarenal or perinephric abscess or obstruction
Sepsis or septic shock arising from any GNB focus (organ dysfunction, hypotension)

Community-acquired pyogenic liver abscess in a patient without hepatobiliary disease, especially of Asian background and/or diabetic, raising concern for hvKp with metastatic spread (endophthalmitis, CNS abscess, necrotizing fasciitis)
Grossly bloody diarrhea without fever, suggesting STEC/EHEC and risk of hemolytic-uremic syndrome
Myositis or fasciitis of the thigh due to E. coli, which should prompt a search for an abdominal source spreading contiguously
Neonatal infection (bacteremia, necrotizing enterocolitis, meningitis), including Cronobacter sakazakii linked to contaminated powdered infant formula
harrison.prognosis: Outcomes correlate with severity of illness, underlying host status, and the resistance profile of the infecting organism, which can lead to suboptimal therapy. Pneumonia, sepsis, and septic shock from any GNB focus carry mortality rates of roughly 20 to 60 percent; ExPEC pneumonia specifically has high crude (20-60%) and attributable (10-20%) mortality. Uncomplicated cystitis is largely self-limited and rarely progresses, whereas pyelonephritis can take 5-7 days for fever to resolve even with effective therapy and only uncommonly causes renal parenchymal loss (mainly with obstruction). hvKp infections can be life- and organ-threatening even in young healthy hosts, with survivors often left with catastrophic sequelae such as vision loss or major neurologic deficits. Pandrug-resistant strains exist, and extensive resistance can leave few or no ideal therapeutic options.
pitfalls: Treating colonization rather than true infection (e.g., asymptomatic bacteriuria or a positive sputum culture without pneumonia), which drives resistance and harm without benefit

Attributing E. coli bacteremia to a urinary source in the absence of characteristic UTI signs, especially given high rates of asymptomatic bacteriuria in elderly and functionally compromised patients, thereby missing an occult abdominal focus

Relying on third-generation cephalosporins for organisms prone to inducible/derepressed AmpC beta-lactamase (e.g., Enterobacter cloacae, Klebsiella aerogenes, Citrobacter freundii), in which resistance can emerge during therapy and cause clinical failure, particularly in bacteremia
Giving antibiotics for STEC/EHEC infection, which may increase the incidence of HUS through increased Shiga toxin release

Assuming carbapenems cover all Enterobacterales: Proteus, Morganella, and Providencia are intrinsically resistant to imipenem, and tetracycline derivatives and polymyxins are poorly active against the tribe Proteeae and Serratia and may achieve inadequate urine/blood levels
Failing to achieve source control (abscess drainage, debridement of necrotic tissue, removal of infected foreign bodies), without which antimicrobial therapy often fails
Empirical reliance on fluoroquinolones in critically ill patients, which is now unreliable given widespread GNB resistance often linked to ESBL production
harrison.severityClassification: Disease is stratified clinically rather than by a single formal score: localized/uncomplicated infection (e.g., uncomplicated cystitis with dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain) versus systemic/severe infection (febrile or systemic UTI/urosepsis, pyelonephritis, prostatitis, pneumonia, bacteremia, sepsis syndrome defined as dysfunction of at least one organ/system, and septic shock). Resistance is graded as multidrug-resistant (MDR), extensively drug-resistant (XDR), and pandrug-resistant; resistance mechanisms range from broad-spectrum beta-lactamases through ESBLs and AmpC enzymes to carbapenemases (Ambler class A serine [KPC], class B metallo-beta-lactamases [NDM, VIM, IMP], and class D [OXA-48]).
management: Prompt empirical broad-spectrum antimicrobials active against Enterobacterales, taking cultures first, then de-escalating to susceptibility-directed therapy
Source control, including drainage of abscesses, removal of infected catheters and devices and relief of urinary or biliary obstruction
Early sepsis resuscitation and organ support for severe sepsis and septic shock
Tailor therapy to the resistance profile, using carbapenems for extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producers and newer beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations for carbapenemase producers
Avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents in Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli enteritis because of the risk of precipitating haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Cross-sectional imaging to identify occult sources such as intra-abdominal abscesses underlying bacteraemia
Infection prevention and control with isolation and screening for carbapenemase-producing organisms, supported by antimicrobial stewardship
